The AutoType Framework

Source: vignettes/autotype-framework.Rmd
autotype-framework.Rmd

Writing a detector that accepts real values is easy. The hard part is rejecting plausible-but-wrong ones — a string that is the right data type but breaks the format. A detector that only ever saw positives has no way to know whether its rule is too loose. The AutoType framework closes that gap: it synthesizes hard negatives from a handful of positives, so a detector can be scored for both recall (accepts real values) and precision (rejects near-misses). It is the engine behind the bundled data_type_tests fixtures and the stress-test grid, and the tool you reach for when refining a mask. (For the kinds of structure detectors key on, see vignette("detector-kinds"); for the catalogue, vignette("data-type-detectors").)

The method reimplements AutoType (Yan & He, Auto-Type: Synthesizing Type-Detection Logic …, SIGMOD 2018); the functions live in R/00-autotype-functions.R.

Four tiers of hard negatives

Starting from real positives, AutoType mutates each one into near-misses along four tiers, each aimed at a different part of the format’s structure:

Tier Name What it changes Structure it stresses
S1 preserve-structure replaces only alphanumerics, delimiters stay put the values (often regenerates a valid value for loose types)
S2 preserve-alphabet replaces any char, but only with characters seen in the positives the arrangement, staying in-vocabulary
S3 random replaces characters with arbitrary printable ASCII the alphabet itself (the easiest negatives)
SP scramble-structure keeps the alphanumerics and their order, permutes where the punctuation sits the format style directly

SP is the sharpest tool. It holds the data type constant and attacks only the placement of delimiters — a decimal point, a grouping comma, a dash in the wrong spot — catching a detector that checks “the right characters are present” but not “in the right places”. In that sense the fixtures test formats more than types.

Generating and reading a fixture

Three steps: generate negatives, score a detector, read the report.

P <- c("ENSG00000139618", "ENSMUSG00000102659", "ENST00000407559")

# one tier at a time ...
generate_autotype_negatives(P, tier = "SP", n_per_positive = 5, seed = 514)

# ... or the full valid + S1/S2/S3/SP fixture as a labelled table
cases <- generate_autotype_test_cases(P, data_type = "ensembl_id")

# score a detector against it and read recall + per-tier false-positive rates
res <- build_autotype_results(is_ensembl_id, P)
autotype_summary(res)
#>    type  n pass_rate
#>   valid  3      1.00   <- recall: must be 1.00
#>      S1 ..      ...    <- share of near-misses WRONGLY accepted (lower better)
#>      S2 ..      ...
#>      S3 ..      ...
#>      SP ..      ...
generate_autotype_report(res, "ensembl_id")   # lists the actual false positives

Read the table as:

  • Recall (the valid row) should be 1.00 — a detector that rejects real values is broken.
  • S1/S2/S3/SP are false-positive rates: near-misses the detector wrongly accepted. Lower is better; blank means the tier produced no distinct negatives.
  • A high S1 is expected for loose formats — mutating the digits of $12.30 to $47.99 just makes another valid amount. Read S2/S3/SP for those.

Refining a mask

This is the loop the framework is built for. A regex that is too permissive shows up as SP false positives: the characters are right, the layout is wrong, and the detector accepts it anyway.

ein <- c("12-3456789", "98-7654321", "04-2103594", "53-0196605", "13-1624016")

# too loose: "any two groups of digits around a dash" also accepts "123-456789"
is_ein_loose <- function(x) grepl("^[0-9]+-[0-9]+$", x)
autotype_summary(build_autotype_results(is_ein_loose, ein))
#> high SP: "12-3456789" scrambled to "123-456789" still passes

# tightened to the real shape: two digits, dash, seven digits
is_ein_tight <- function(x) grepl("^[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{7}$", x)
autotype_summary(build_autotype_results(is_ein_tight, ein))
#> SP drops toward 0; recall stays 1.00

Iterate: run the fixture, find the tier that leaks, tighten the rule toward the positional structure (a {n} count, an anchored prefix, a checksum), and re-run until recall is 1.00 and SP is near 0. generate_autotype_report() prints the specific near-misses that still pass, so each iteration has a concrete target.

From fixtures to the stress-test grid

The per-detector fixture above tests a detector in isolation. The production-scale extension perturbs whole banked columns and measures how column-level accuracy decays — an experimental design on top of fx_benchmark() (see vignette("benchmarking")). It reuses the same mutation module and adds column-level dimensions, each at graded levels:

Dimension What it does
spelling class-preserving substitution (digit↔︎digit, letter↔︎letter)
length resample the column to N in {50, 100, 300}
contamination mix in foil values from another type (10% / 25%)
whitespace, case, static stray padding, random case folding, stray punctuation
missingness inject sentinels ("", NA, -, null)
scramble_punct, scramble_alnum permute punctuation (reuses SP) / alphanumerics 
# perturb a single column along one dimension x level ...
fx_perturb(iso_date, dimension = "scramble_punct", level = "medium", seed = 514)

# ... or run the whole grid over the banked columns and read the decay
grid <- fx_stress_grid()
fx_stress_summary(grid)   # accuracy per dimension x level x data_type

Reading the decay per dimension tells you which robustness a type lacks, which points back to exactly the mask-refinement loop above.
